fields.label: Topic summary
fields.value: Lua is a compact, portable, dynamically typed multi-paradigm language designed for embedding and extending host applications. Its small core, tables, first-class functions, closures, metatables, bytecode VM, and C API enable a wide range of programming patterns and integrations.

value.name: Source-to-VM execution pipeline
value.mechanism: Source text is compiled to bytecode; the VM executes bytecode. Compilation may happen at runtime or offline, and JIT implementations may compile code to native instructions.
conditions: Standard Lua bytecode execution model described by the article
JIT behavior varies by implementation

value.name: Embedded-language integration model
value.mechanism: The host creates a Lua state and uses the C API to load scripts and exchange values, enabling extension without moving the entire application into Lua.
conditions: Host application integrates the C API
Host explicitly exposes capabilities to scripts

value.name: C API call stack model
value.mechanism: The C API stack is the transfer mechanism for arguments and results; the example calls foo(5,3) and reads 8.
conditions: C program invokes a Lua function through the stack API

value.name: Table-based object model
value.mechanism: An object's table stores its fields; metatable lookup delegates missing methods to a prototype table.
conditions: The programmer implements this pattern; it is not a built-in class system

value.name: Table reference and aliasing model
value.mechanism: Both variables refer to the same table object, so a field mutation is visible through both references.
conditions: No copy/clone operation is performed

value.name: Closure capture model
value.mechanism: Each invocation of addto creates a function retaining access to that invocation's x value.
conditions: The returned function references a local from its defining lexical scope

value.name: Metatable-driven memoization
value.mechanism: A metatable's __index function handles missing keys and writes computed values into the table.
conditions: The metatable is attached to fibs
Required lower Fibonacci values are available or recursively computed

value.name: Lua control-flow selection
value.mechanism: Explicit then/end delimit conditional blocks, while optional else/elseif supply alternatives.
conditions: A conditional expression is evaluated

value.name: Lua loop families
value.mechanism: Lua provides four loop forms in the article's taxonomy, each suited to different termination or iteration logic.
conditions: Loop body and termination condition are correctly specified

value.name: Table as universal composite data model
value.mechanism: The same table primitive represents heterogeneous associative arrays, sequences, records, nested structures, namespaces, and object fields.
conditions: Programmer defines conventions for keys and shape

value.name: Lua module loading model
steps: Search/load Lua module or native extension
value.mechanism: Lua's module system can load Lua modules or native shared objects; native modules conventionally expose luaopen_foo.
conditions: Module is discoverable and compatible with the active runtime

value.name: Managed object lifetime
value.mechanism: Lua garbage collection manages objects such as closures and avoids requiring the host C program to manually reference-count every Lua object.
conditions: Object is managed by the Lua runtime

value.name: Lua dialect and target-language relationships
value.mechanism: Luau, Ravi, Teal, Pluto, GLua, PICO-8 Lua, LuaJIT and other variants differ in compatibility, typing, syntax, performance or host-specific APIs.
conditions: Features are dialect/version-specific; do not assume every implementation supports all extensions

value.name: Historical influence graph
steps: Syntax and semantics influenced by other languages
value.mechanism: Lua's design emerged from practical embedding requirements and selective borrowing from earlier languages rather than adopting a single paradigm wholesale.
conditions: Historical details are limited to the supplied article

value.name: Game scripting integration
value.mechanism: Lua's embedding design allows game developers to expose scriptable behavior while retaining core engine functionality in native code.
conditions: A game uses Lua or a dialect and exposes a scripting API

value.name: Lua typing profile
steps: Variables may refer to different types over time
value.mechanism: The article characterizes base Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed while also describing coercion; dialects such as Luau and Ravi add other typing features.
conditions: Typing behavior and extensions vary by Lua version/dialect

conditions: Bytecode compatibility depends on implementation/version; source excerpt does not detail compatibility rules

value.name: Namespace via table
value.mechanism: A table containing related functions can act as a namespace without requiring a dedicated namespace construct.

value.distinction: Embedding describes how the runtime is integrated into a host; extension describes the purpose of allowing users to add behavior to that host.
Lua source is human-readable text; bytecode is the compiled VM instruction representation.
The Lua VM executes bytecode as a software runtime; the CPU executes native instructions implementing that runtime.
Lua's VM is described as register-based, while the C API used to exchange values is stack-based; these are different layers and do not conflict.
Base Lua is described as dynamically typed; Luau adds gradual typing as a dialect feature.
An array is a usage pattern of a general key-value table, not a separate built-in composite type.
Assigning a table variable copies a reference; creating a new table constructor creates a distinct table.
nil denotes an absent table value; a nil gap in a sequence can make the # length result ambiguous.
Dot syntax is shorthand for a string-key lookup and does not introduce a separate field-storage mechanism.
A closure is a function that retains access to lexical variables from its defining environment.
Lua's examples use prototype delegation; class-like APIs are programmer-built conventions rather than a built-in class construct.
A metatable is the table of customization rules; a metamethod is a named hook such as __index or __add.
Coroutines provide cooperative task switching; the source does not describe them as operating-system threads.
The baseline execution model compiles to VM bytecode; a JIT is an implementation technique that can compile code during execution.
The core API provides base functionality; the auxiliary library supplies helper operations and macros.
Luau derives from Lua 5.1 and adds dialect-specific typing, performance, and sandbox features; it is not identical to every Lua version.
require is the loading interface; a native extension is a compiled shared object that exposes an entry point such as luaopen_foo.
A namespace table is a programming convention built using a general table, not a dedicated namespace primitive.
Source claims capture what the article states; formal models may organize those statements into explanatory pipelines.
A named stable Lua version and an implementation targeting an older language version are different kinds of release identity.

value.misconception: Lua has separate built-in array, record, and object composite types.
value.correction: The source describes tables as the only built-in composite type; arrays, records, namespaces, and objects are patterns built with tables.

value.misconception: Lua has native class declarations like class-based languages.
value.correction: The article says Lua has no built-in class concept in the described model; class-like behavior is emulated with tables, functions, and metatables.

value.misconception: Lua source text is executed directly without compilation.
value.correction: The article states that Lua source is compiled into bytecode that runs on the Lua VM.

value.misconception: Lua's VM and C API both use the same stack architecture.
value.correction: The VM is described as register-based, whereas the C API uses a stack to exchange values.

value.misconception: Lua's automatic sequence indexing starts at zero.
value.correction: The source says automatic array-style indexing starts at 1, although explicit key 0 is legal.

value.misconception: The # operator always returns an unambiguous count for any table.
value.correction: The article notes that tables with holes can have more than one valid boundary for the length operator.

value.misconception: Assigning one table variable to another clones the table.
value.correction: The source example shows both variables referring to the same table; mutation through one is visible through the other.

value.misconception: Metatables are only for object-oriented programming.
value.correction: The source shows metatables also supporting missing-key lookup, memoization, operator overloading, and semantic customization.

value.misconception: A returned function loses access to its outer local when the outer call returns.
value.correction: The closure example retains access to its own captured x value, managed by the garbage collector.

value.misconception: Lua is used only for games.
value.correction: The article lists editors, web servers, databases, packet analyzers, typesetting, and MediaWiki among non-game uses.

value.misconception: Luau, LuaJIT, Teal, and standard Lua are identical implementations.
value.correction: The article describes dialects/implementations with different compatibility, typing, performance, syntax, or sandbox behavior.

value.misconception: Embedding Lua requires manual reference counting for every Lua object.
value.correction: The article explicitly contrasts Lua's C API with APIs that require manual reference counting.

value.misconception: Dynamic typing necessarily means weak typing.
value.correction: The source metadata describes Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed, and separately lists supported runtime coercion; these labels are not synonyms.

value.misconception: Lua includes every advanced feature as a fixed built-in construct.
value.correction: The design emphasizes small extensible meta-features, with classes and inheritance implemented by conventions rather than dedicated constructs.

value.misconception: Coroutines automatically provide preemptive parallel threads.
value.correction: The source characterizes coroutines as cooperative multitasking; it does not claim OS-thread parallelism.

source_claims.claim: Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm language designed mainly for embedding in applications.
Lua was created in 1993 at Tecgraf by Roberto Ierusalimschy, Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo, and Waldemar Celes.
SOL and DEL were predecessor configuration/data-description languages whose limitations motivated a more expressive language.
Lua favors a small base language and extensible meta-features over a large set of paradigm-specific built-ins.
Tables are Lua's only built-in composite type and support associative arrays, records, arrays, namespaces, and objects.
First-class functions, lexical scoping, and closures support higher-order programming and information hiding.
Metatables customize table behavior and enable lookup delegation, memoization, operator overloading, and object-oriented patterns.
Lua source is compiled to bytecode for a register-based virtual machine; compilation may occur at runtime or offline.
The C API is stack-based and provides core and auxiliary libraries for embedding and calling Lua from C.
Lua can load Lua modules and native shared-object extensions, with LuaRocks providing package management.
Lua is widely used in game development due to its embeddability, execution speed, and short learning curve.
The article lists non-game applications such as Lightroom, LuaTeX, Redis, Neovim, Nginx, Wireshark, and MediaWiki Scribunto.
Lua has derivatives and dialects that differ in typing, performance, syntax, compatibility, and host integration.
Lua versions before 5.0 used a BSD-like license; versions from 5.0 onward use the MIT License.
The article says the register-based VM can reduce value copying and the number of instructions per function compared with stack-based VM architectures.
Luau is described as a Lua 5.1 derivative with gradual typing, performance focus, and improved sandboxing for untrusted scripts.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua has separate built-in array, record, and object composite types.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes tables as the only built-in composite type; arrays, records, namespaces, and objects are patterns built with tables.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua has native class declarations like class-based languages.
misconceptions.correction: The article says Lua has no built-in class concept in the described model; class-like behavior is emulated with tables, functions, and metatables.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua source text is executed directly without compilation.
misconceptions.correction: The article states that Lua source is compiled into bytecode that runs on the Lua VM.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua's VM and C API both use the same stack architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The VM is described as register-based, whereas the C API uses a stack to exchange values.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua's automatic sequence indexing starts at zero.
misconceptions.correction: The source says automatic array-style indexing starts at 1, although explicit key 0 is legal.

misconceptions.misconception: The # operator always returns an unambiguous count for any table.
misconceptions.correction: The article notes that tables with holes can have more than one valid boundary for the length operator.

misconceptions.misconception: Assigning one table variable to another clones the table.
misconceptions.correction: The source example shows both variables referring to the same table; mutation through one is visible through the other.

misconceptions.misconception: Metatables are only for object-oriented programming.
misconceptions.correction: The source shows metatables also supporting missing-key lookup, memoization, operator overloading, and semantic customization.

misconceptions.misconception: A returned function loses access to its outer local when the outer call returns.
misconceptions.correction: The closure example retains access to its own captured x value, managed by the garbage collector.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua is used only for games.
misconceptions.correction: The article lists editors, web servers, databases, packet analyzers, typesetting, and MediaWiki among non-game uses.

misconceptions.misconception: Luau, LuaJIT, Teal, and standard Lua are identical implementations.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes dialects/implementations with different compatibility, typing, performance, syntax, or sandbox behavior.

misconceptions.misconception: Embedding Lua requires manual reference counting for every Lua object.
misconceptions.correction: The article explicitly contrasts Lua's C API with APIs that require manual reference counting.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic typing necessarily means weak typing.
misconceptions.correction: The source metadata describes Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed, and separately lists supported runtime coercion; these labels are not synonyms.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua includes every advanced feature as a fixed built-in construct.
misconceptions.correction: The design emphasizes small extensible meta-features, with classes and inheritance implemented by conventions rather than dedicated constructs.

misconceptions.misconception: Coroutines automatically provide preemptive parallel threads.
misconceptions.correction: The source characterizes coroutines as cooperative multitasking; it does not claim OS-thread parallelism.

value.misconception: A switch simply repeats every frame to all ports.
value.correction: A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and selectively forwards frames where forwarding state permits; hubs repeat traffic broadly.

value.misconception: Switches eliminate all broadcast traffic.
value.correction: Switch ports separate collision domains, but broadcasts are still forwarded within the broadcast domain.

value.misconception: Every network switch routes IP packets.
value.correction: Ordinary Ethernet switches commonly operate at Layer 2; Layer 3/multilayer switches add routing functionality.

value.misconception: MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable.
value.correction: MAC addresses guide link-layer forwarding; IP addresses support network-layer routing.

value.misconception: STP forwards on every redundant link.
value.correction: STP disables forwarding on selected links to create a loop-free active topology; SPB/TRILL are alternatives described as allowing multiple active paths.

value.misconception: A VLAN is a separate physical switch.
value.correction: A VLAN is logical Layer 2 segmentation that can be configured and tagged on managed switches.

value.misconception: Smart and enterprise switches have the same feature set.
value.correction: Smart switches offer limited features; enterprise switches provide broader configuration and monitoring capabilities.

value.misconception: Any device on a switch can sniff all switched traffic.
value.correction: Ordinary visibility is limited to relevant ports; port mirroring, taps, hubs or monitoring systems are used to observe additional traffic.

value.misconception: Cut-through waits for the entire frame before forwarding.
value.correction: Cut-through can begin forwarding after enough header data has arrived to make the decision.

value.misconception: PoE and UPS mean the same thing.
value.correction: PoE powers compatible endpoints over Ethernet; UPS backs up power to keep the switch and attached devices running during power loss.

value.misconception: The MAC table and CAM are exactly the same kind of thing.
value.correction: The MAC table is the logical mapping; CAM is a common high-speed hardware implementation.

value.misconception: Every switch port must use fiber modules.
value.correction: Switch interfaces can use different media; the source describes pluggable optics and DAC copper alternatives.

value.misconception: Full-duplex point-to-point links behave like shared half-duplex segments.
value.correction: The article says full-duplex has simultaneous transmit/receive and makes collisions impossible in the described model.

value.misconception: A managed switch by itself guarantees network security.
value.correction: ACLs, MAC filtering, 802.1X, VLANs, firewall and IDS integrations are features or controls, not a universal security guarantee.

value.misconception: Every internal switch hardware detail is explicitly specified by the article.
value.correction: CAM and transceivers/CPO are mentioned explicitly; detailed switch-fabric, ASIC pipeline and plane-separation descriptions are labeled engineering synthesis.

source_claims.claim: A network switch is a multiport bridge that forwards traffic toward destination devices, typically using MAC addresses at Layer 2.
Unlike a repeater hub, a switch learns device addresses and forwards data toward the destination port rather than repeating everything to all ports.
Each switch port forms a separate collision domain in the described Ethernet model, while broadcasts remain within the broadcast domain.
Switches may use SFP and other pluggable transceiver modules, DAC cables and co-packaged optics.
Some switches add Layer 3 routing and are called Layer 3 or multilayer switches.
The MAC address table maps MAC addresses to ports and is often implemented with high-speed CAM.
Cut-through switches may begin forwarding before the entire frame payload has arrived, reducing latency.
STP disables forwarding on selected links to avoid switching loops; SPB and TRILL are described as alternatives supporting active paths.
PoE can power endpoints such as VoIP phones and wireless access points; UPS-backed switch power can support continuity.
Managed switch features include VLANs, link aggregation, QoS, ACLs, SNMP, port mirroring, NTP, 802.1X, LLDP and IGMP snooping.
Port mirroring sends a copy of selected traffic to a monitoring port; alternatives include SMON, RMON, sFlow, a network tap or a Layer 1 hub.
The article credits Mark Kempf/DEC with the 1983 MAC bridge and dates Kalpana's seven-port EtherSwitch to 1989–1990.
The article warns that its lead may be too technical for most readers.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Switch learns addresses and selectively forwards where possible; hub repeats traffic out all other ports.
Layer 2 switching uses MAC addresses; Layer 3 switching adds routing functionality.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Clarifies forwarding key and protocol layer.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Switch ports separate collision domains, but broadcasts still propagate within the broadcast domain.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Avoids confusing collision reduction with broadcast containment.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: MAC addresses guide Layer 2 forwarding; IP addresses are used for network-layer routing.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates local-link delivery from inter-network routing.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Data plane forwards frames; control protocols such as STP determine topology and forwarding eligibility.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Useful for debugging forwarding versus topology convergence.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Managed models expose configuration and monitoring; unmanaged models are plug-and-play.
Smart switches offer limited controls; enterprise switches expose broader CLI/SNMP/web management and configuration lifecycle features.
Port mirroring copies traffic within switch configuration; a tap is an external hardware monitoring method.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Explains visibility methods and failure domains.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Cut-through starts forwarding before the full payload arrives; buffering/store-forward waits longer but can support different handling.
STP forms a loop-free tree by disabling selected links; SPB/TRILL are described as alternatives allowing multiple paths active.
A VLAN is logical segmentation; a port is a physical/logical interface and may be assigned to a VLAN.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates logical topology from physical interface.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: An optical module/transceiver connects an interface to fiber; a supported DAC cable can replace a module for copper connectivity.
PoE delivers power over Ethernet to endpoints; UPS provides backup power to the switch/power system.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates endpoint power delivery from power continuity.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Traditional Layer 2 switching bridges MAC-addressed frames; routers interconnect at Layer 3; multilayer switches may combine functions.
MAC table is logical mapping state; CAM is one hardware implementation for high-speed lookup.

misconceptions.misconception: A switch simply repeats every frame to all ports.
misconceptions.correction: A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and selectively forwards frames where forwarding state permits; hubs repeat traffic broadly.

misconceptions.misconception: Switches eliminate all broadcast traffic.
misconceptions.correction: Switch ports separate collision domains, but broadcasts are still forwarded within the broadcast domain.

misconceptions.misconception: Every network switch routes IP packets.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary Ethernet switches commonly operate at Layer 2; Layer 3/multilayer switches add routing functionality.

misconceptions.misconception: MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: MAC addresses guide link-layer forwarding; IP addresses support network-layer routing.

misconceptions.misconception: STP forwards on every redundant link.
misconceptions.correction: STP disables forwarding on selected links to create a loop-free active topology; SPB/TRILL are alternatives described as allowing multiple active paths.

misconceptions.misconception: A VLAN is a separate physical switch.
misconceptions.correction: A VLAN is logical Layer 2 segmentation that can be configured and tagged on managed switches.

misconceptions.misconception: Smart and enterprise switches have the same feature set.
misconceptions.correction: Smart switches offer limited features; enterprise switches provide broader configuration and monitoring capabilities.

misconceptions.misconception: Any device on a switch can sniff all switched traffic.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary visibility is limited to relevant ports; port mirroring, taps, hubs or monitoring systems are used to observe additional traffic.

misconceptions.misconception: Cut-through waits for the entire frame before forwarding.
misconceptions.correction: Cut-through can begin forwarding after enough header data has arrived to make the decision.

misconceptions.misconception: PoE and UPS mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: PoE powers compatible endpoints over Ethernet; UPS backs up power to keep the switch and attached devices running during power loss.

misconceptions.misconception: The MAC table and CAM are exactly the same kind of thing.
misconceptions.correction: The MAC table is the logical mapping; CAM is a common high-speed hardware implementation.

misconceptions.misconception: Every switch port must use fiber modules.
misconceptions.correction: Switch interfaces can use different media; the source describes pluggable optics and DAC copper alternatives.

misconceptions.misconception: Full-duplex point-to-point links behave like shared half-duplex segments.
misconceptions.correction: The article says full-duplex has simultaneous transmit/receive and makes collisions impossible in the described model.

misconceptions.misconception: A managed switch by itself guarantees network security.
misconceptions.correction: ACLs, MAC filtering, 802.1X, VLANs, firewall and IDS integrations are features or controls, not a universal security guarantee.

misconceptions.misconception: Every internal switch hardware detail is explicitly specified by the article.
misconceptions.correction: CAM and transceivers/CPO are mentioned explicitly; detailed switch-fabric, ASIC pipeline and plane-separation descriptions are labeled engineering synthesis.
